newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Sharif takes control of parliament.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Sharif takes control of parliament.

text.p: Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party and its allies won a majority of the Senate (upper house) seats contested on Wednesday, consolidating their hold on the two-chamber parliament.

PML sources said that after the election of about half of 87-seat Senate ended on Wednesday, the party and its allies would have a two-thirds majority in the upper house so they could amend Pakistan's constitution.

They had already won more than a two-thirds majority in the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) in a landslide general election victory on February 3, in which ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) suffered a crushing defeat.
The PML has 30 seats in the Senate after Wednesday's voting for 27 seats by three provincial assemblies of Sindh, North West Frontier and Baluchistan provinces, party sources said.
The PML had already won all the 10 seats from the populous Punjab province and two from the Islamabad capital area without a contest.
A spokesman for Sharif said the party and its allies would have a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which is necessary for any constitutional amendment.
But a question remains whether Sharif will use this majority to remove the controversial constitution clauses that empowers the president to sack a prime minister and dissolve the National Assembly.

That power has been used twice against Bhutto -- in 1990 by then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan and last November by President Farooq Leghari -- and once against Sharif when he was sacked as prime minister in 1993 by Ishaq Khan.
"Parliament is sovereign and the mandate given by people ought to be utilised for the fulfilment of national aspirations," Sharif's press assistant Siddiqul Farooq told Reuters.

"We will use this absolute power absolutely for the betterment of the country and we will not go for confrontation. We will rather, as a matter of policy, take opposition along with us for the implementation of the national agenda," he said.

Bhutto accuses Leghari and a caretaker government he set up after sacking her of rigging the February 3 elections to defeat her but has said she will cooperate with Sharif for the supremacy of parliament.
The government denies the rigging charge.

Pakistan's constitution has set a five-year term of office for a prime minister, but all the four prime ministers who have taken office since 1985 were prematurely sacked by presidents, mainly on disputed grounds of corruption.
